title: Mastery Challenge: Chemistry
objective: After this level you can demonstrate command of Chemistry Levels 1–99 across the whole tree.
summary: Ten questions linking the great chemists to the matter they studied: stills and gases, burning and atoms, radium, DNA, new materials, greener processes and myths. Every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: The Chemistry Mastery Challenge.
cards.body: Ten questions that tie the great chemists back to the matter they studied, from the alchemist's still to the myth of chemical-free. Level 1 asked what chemistry is. Show how far you've come. Take your time: every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: Chemistry: mastered
learned: How chemistry grew from alchemists chasing gold into a science built on careful experiments.
How Lavoisier's weighing and Dalton's atoms showed that reactions rearrange matter and never lose it.
What Curie found in pitchblende, and how Franklin's X-ray photo revealed DNA's helix.
Why nothing is truly chemical-free, and why green chemistry prevents waste instead of cleaning it up.

questions.prompt: Great Chemists mastery: alchemists heated mixtures in an alembic and collected what dripped out. Which Chapter 1 separation is that?

options.label: Filtering
options.rationale: Filtering holds back solids with a filter; no heating or vapor.

options.label: Distilling
Evaporating in an open pan
options.rationale: That lets the vapor escape instead of collecting it.

options.label: Letting it settle
options.rationale: Settling doesn't involve heat or vapor.

questions.explanation: An alembic heats a mixture, cools the vapor and collects the liquid: distillation.

questions.prompt: Great Chemists mastery: a bubble of trapped gas moves to where the pressure on it is half as much, at the same temperature. What does Boyle's law say happens to its volume?

options.label: It halves
options.rationale: Less pressure lets the gas expand, not shrink.

options.label: It stays the same
options.rationale: Volume changes when pressure changes.

options.label: It doubles
It quadruples
options.rationale: Halving the pressure only doubles the volume.

questions.explanation: Volume is inversely proportional to pressure, so half the pressure means twice the volume.

questions.prompt: Great Chemists mastery: which old idea did Lavoisier's experiments with burning metals overturn?

options.label: That matter is made of tiny atoms
options.rationale: Dalton argued for atoms after Lavoisier.

options.label: That air has mass and takes up space
options.rationale: Lavoisier's explanation depended on air having mass.

options.label: That burning things release phlogiston
That gases can be squeezed smaller
options.rationale: That's Boyle's law, which still holds.

questions.explanation: Metals gain mass when they burn because oxygen combines with them, which phlogiston theory couldn't explain.

questions.prompt: Great Chemists mastery: a burning candle turns wax into carbon dioxide and water. What would Dalton say happened to the atoms?

options.label: The flame destroyed them completely
options.rationale: Dalton said atoms are never destroyed.

options.label: They all escaped from the candle as light
options.rationale: The atoms end up in new substances.

options.label: They turned into atoms of new elements
options.rationale: Each element keeps its own kind of atom.

options.label: They rearranged into new substances

questions.explanation: A chemical change rearranges atoms into new substances; in Dalton's theory none are created or destroyed.

questions.prompt: Great Chemists mastery: Marie Curie was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize. What else is she still the only woman to have done?

options.label: Win Nobel Prizes in two different fields
Discover the nucleus at the center of the atom
options.rationale: That wasn't Curie.

options.label: Win the Nobel Prize in Physics outright
options.rationale: Her 1903 physics prize was shared, and other women have won it since.

options.label: Name an element after one of the planets
options.rationale: Polonium is named after Poland.

questions.explanation: She won physics in 1903 and chemistry in 1911, and remains the only woman to win in two fields.

questions.prompt: Great Chemists mastery: which technique did Rosalind Franklin use to study the structure of DNA?

options.label: Distillation
options.rationale: That separates mixtures, Level 7.

options.label: X-ray diffraction
Carbon dating
options.rationale: That tells age, not structure.

options.label: Weighing it on a balance
options.rationale: Mass alone can't show a molecule's shape.

questions.explanation: X-rays scatter off a crystal at angles that reveal how its atoms are arranged, as in Photo 51.

questions.prompt: Great Chemists mastery: what made nylon such a breakthrough compared with silk?

options.label: It was spun by a new breed of silkworm
options.rationale: No silkworms were involved.

options.label: Chemists built it from compounds in air, water, coal or petroleum
It was the very first material people ever wove into cloth
options.rationale: People had woven fibers long before.

options.label: It was found by accident inside a cylinder of stored gas
options.rationale: That was Teflon.

questions.explanation: Nylon was built by chemical synthesis from widely available compounds, a synthetic silk with no silkworms needed.

questions.prompt: Great Chemists mastery: route A makes a medicine with 40 percent of its atoms ending up in the product; route B, 80 percent. Which fits atom economy better?

options.label: Route A, because wasting atoms makes a purer medicine
options.rationale: Wasting atoms is what atom economy avoids.

options.label: Neither, because atom economy is only about speed
options.rationale: It's about where the atoms end up.

options.label: Route B: more starting material ends up in the product
Both, because the medicine is the same either way
options.rationale: Twice as many atoms end up in route B's product.

questions.explanation: Atom economy favors the route whose product keeps more of the starting materials.

questions.prompt: Great Chemists mastery: a bottle of spring water is labeled "no chemicals". What's the best correction?

options.label: Water is matter, and all matter is made of chemicals
Only tap water contains chemicals
options.rationale: Spring water is made of chemicals too.

options.label: The label is right because water is natural
options.rationale: Natural substances are chemicals too.

options.label: Water isn't matter, so the label doesn't matter
options.rationale: Water has mass and takes up space.

questions.explanation: Everything you drink is made of chemicals: water itself is matter, made of chemicals.

questions.prompt: Great Chemists mastery: Dalton studied the gases of the air. Why does Chapter 1 call air a solution?

options.label: It is always damp, and solutions must be wet
options.rationale: Solutions don't need to be liquid.

options.label: Its gases are evenly mixed all the way through
It contains only one pure substance, oxygen
options.rationale: Air is mostly nitrogen and oxygen.

options.label: It can be poured from one jar to another
options.rationale: Air flows, but that's not what makes it a solution.

questions.explanation: Air is a homogeneous mixture of mostly nitrogen and oxygen, evenly mixed, so it is a solution.
